items.author: danielfoster
items.content:
FirstDateback in April

How will the matchmaking work? What questions are even in the matchmaking questionnaire? (Read on for the full list)

On FirstDate’s website, one line stands out: “FirstDate uses a Nobel prize-winning framework called the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm”. It’s a brow-raising detail because, despite the name, the algorithm has almost nothing to do with marriage, but more on this later.

The dating service will use Singpass to verify the identity of users, match people in cycles (you get only one match each cycle), and share contact details only when both users agree to their match.

To get a sense of how the matchmaking works, here’s the questionnaire that the government workers signing up must fill out. The questions are a mix of close-ended and open-ended ones, across 8 categories, spanning topics like interests and passions, lifestyle and daily habits, and communication and relationship style.

  1. What are you into these days?

  2. Now, spill! What do you actually love about your hobbies?

  3. What cuisines do you eat on repeat and never get sick of?

  4. Which restaurant do you keep going back to and why?

  5. How often do you find an excuse to leave the country?

  6. What kind of traveler are you, really?

  7. What’s a country that’s ruined all other countries for you?

  8. Team sunrise, or team “it’s 2am and I’m still up”?

  9. Gym rat, occasional jogger, or exercise is a myth to you?

  10. Any food rules we should know about?

  11. Be honest! What does your room look like right now?

  12. Hustle mode, or protecting your personal time?

  13. Real talk. How much of your day disappears into your phone?

  14. Describe your social energy. Are you the life of the party, or the one who left an hour ago?

  15. How important is it for you that a match brings the same energy, or do opposites attract for you?

  16. After a brutal work week, what’s your reset button?

  17. New city, new hobby, new anything. How do you feel about the unknown?

  18. When you’re feeling a lot, what do you actually do about it?

  19. How do you like to be loved?

  20. Non-stop texting, or comfortable silence. Where do you land?

  21. Mid-disagreement, what’s your gut instinct?

  22. Paint us a picture. What does your dream first date look like?

  23. What are your non-negotiable green flags in a partner?

  24. Are you always working on yourself, or is “good enough” good enough?

  25. Do you see yourself having children?

  26. Saver, spender, or “I’ll figure it out eventually”?

  27. What’s your religion, if any?

  28. Any hard nos for you? Be honest, we won’t judge.

  29. What’s the youngest age you’d consider dating?

  30. What’s the oldest age you’d consider dating?

  31. Write a short note for your future match! Tell us about yourself in a few sentences.

After a question about the name you prefer to go by and your mobile number, the questionnaire also collects information about how many first dates you’ve been on in the past year, whether you’ve used a dating app or matchmaking service before, and when you last went on a first date.

But how will the rest of the data collected through these questions be used? The fascinating history of the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage Algorithm (also known as the deferred acceptance algorithm) gives us some clues.

Before the algorithm earned its name, a similar system was used to match medical school residents with residency programmes in hospitals in the United States since the 1950s. After an interview process, doctors and hospitals provide a rank ordered list of their preferences, which the algorithm turns into a stable match.

What makes the match stable is that after all the matching has concluded, no pair would rather be paired with one another over their current partners.

Confused? This YouTube video explains it better than I can:

What made the algorithm so novel was that it proved that such a stable match always exists when there are equal participants of each type (and that there is a solution to achieve it). The 2012 Nobel Prize in economics went to one of the mathematicians who developed the algorithm (Shapley) and an economist who pointed out the medical resident example and used it to develop other real world applications.

It’s called a marriage algorithm because the theory used marriage proposals as a memorable but theoretical example. The real world applications of the algorithm (like school choice systems) tend to have little to do with dating, for reasons that I’ll elaborate on below.

What does this mean for those signing up to FirstDate? Well, the algorithm is why FirstDate’s matching takes place in what its developers call “cycles” or “programmatic rounds”.

Presumably, the algorithm uses each user’s questionnaire answers to rank all participants of the opposite gender based on compatibility. The algorithm then matches everyone until all couples are in stable matches (see above).

After you decide to say yes or no to your match, that’s it for the cycle. You’ll have to wait for the next one to get a new stable match with a new pool of participants.

From my perspective, there are three glaring issues that emerge when applying this kind of game theory to dating:

(Side note: While the nature of the algorithm might imply that same-sex pairings are not possible, other dating-related implementations of the algorithm have allowed for same-sex pairings. It is doubtful that this will happen here though, because, well, Singapore.)

All of this is further complicated when there are outside options. Like, say, other online dating services or your workplace crush who isn’t participating in the process. Because there is no commitment to the process (because this isn’t your state-assigned waifu, thank god), the maths that underpins the algorithm doesn’t really make sense.

claims

In short, stable matches mean nothing when nobody is committed and the best options might exist outside of the matchmaking pool.

interviewedAphrodite Project

If you’re a gym rat, does that mean you also want to match with other gym rats?

The problem with modern dating is a problem of mismatched preferences!

According to FirstDate’s website, it “started with a question among a group of GovTech officers: does having more potential matches necessarily make it easier to find a suitable match?”

This is a similar diagnosis to what the folks behind the Aphrodite Project came to, but I feel that it captures an incomplete part of the whole picture.

The rise of online dating paralleled the rise of a particular way of thinking about love that’s more checklist oriented than it is holistic, where daters increasingly screen their options ahead of time against a predetermined list of green and red flags.

How does a system for matchmaking people account for the fact that the people who need matchmaking also tend to be the worst at understanding what they really want in a relationship?

Let me paint you a picture of what seems to be the common dating experience in Singapore: You’re on a first date with someone in a chain restaurant in a mall somewhere in central Singapore. The conversation revolves almost entirely around the biodata and information that HR and recruiters would collect from you.

Where do you live? Where did you study? What job do you have?

There’s nothing innately wrong with having preferences relating to these things, but dating that’s all about these preferences betrays a deeply transactional and instrumentalist view of love that sees other people not as potential life partners, but pathways to potential lifestyles. Not lovers, but co-owners of a financial venture. Not people, but breeders of sought-after children.

It’s a mindset that’s enabled by the market-driven logic of dating apps, where we commodify ourselves to score swipes. It’s also a mindset that gives intensely unattractive only child energy.

In Singapore, this transactional view is only sharpened and reinforced by policies like the BTO system for public housing, where the rational move for financially savvy couples is to apply before marriage, often while one is still studying, so that they can get the best subsidies.

For these couples, it means that they’ll likely have spent no time at all living with their partner-to-be, and navigating messy questions of how you actually are in states of boredom and stress. Instead, they’re spending all their time planning for their financial futures and screening their partner in terms of their viability for a rigid life path.

increase the fertility rate

It is also telling that before the launch of FirstDate, its developers sent out a survey to prospective users on CrowdTask (the government’s survey platform) asking them why they want to be in a relationship.

Perhaps that’s filed under “other” or “enjoying romantic intimacy”?

tend to have similar valueslove language

What I am saying is that perhaps, we shouldn’t be treating our choice of partners with the same mindset as how we approach schools and jobs, through the lens of competition in pursuit of optimal choices. Or through an algorithm used for matching people to their schools and workplaces.

To be clear, I do think that this GovTech pilot programme is an admirable initiative. More experimentation in the public sector is always a net positive, and I hope this doesn’t read as me just clowning on a good faith attempt at fixing what’s wrong with online dating.

There are clear benefits to a model of online dating driven less by profit incentives and shareholder value, and driven more by user needs.

‘Single, Desperate and Ugly’

points out

Still, if the goal of FirstDate is to make a better product than dating apps, they’ve already succeeded (for hetero sinkies aged 21 to 35). But, mind you, the bar is in hell.

enshittification

I’m not convinced that a better algorithm is the solution (though I’d be glad to be proven wrong). Really, the clamouring for it is symptomatic of our redpilled and incel-inflected times.

The truth is that we don’t really know what exactly makes love work, such that we can articulate and implement it on a societal scale. It’s too messy, too complex, too idiosyncratic, and too human. Anyone who claims otherwise probably has a course to sell you on negging and pickup artistry.

I bought the meals, spent so much time offering my shoulder to them, gave so much of myself to them, and they still chose someone else. they’re all just gold diggers, people only value appearance, nice guys finish last.

(I want to scream: love is not a rank ordered list!!)interviewing incels and former incels

Rather than creating an off-ramp from a system of alienating self-commodification, FirstDate creates another platform for people to game.

There’s a good reason why Singaporeans are still – according to surveys by the National Population and Talent Division at least – more likely to find love through offline methods (their schools, workplaces, family friends) than online channels.

declining

The urge to quantify compatibility is understandable. This is Singapore after all, a country where we just can’t resist tying our self worth to a score. But, even a casual look around you at the couples that do work would tell you that this impulse to quantify defies logic.

If the man I’m marrying in January were to fill out this questionnaire, he’d probably fill it out like an introspective soft boy and express a preference for softspoken people that fit into that lifestyle.

(as a queer person, this is strictly a hypothetical)

The result would likely mean being matched up to somebody like our exes.

Instead, we met over Grindr, an app where one has little to go off of besides appearance, distance, and sexual compatibility. And over the next year, he became my plus one to all the nightclubs and bars and parties I write about as a lifestyle journalist. And he, in turn, drags me out to the fandom conventions and game jams that he loves (and that I admittedly am lukewarm on). I fell in love with him on the dancefloor, and he fell in love with me during the quiet times in between.

I’d argue this surprise and unpredictability is key to finding chemistry.

spend so much time in the rat race

So, here’s my proposal: Let’s fund culture clubs, theatre groups, video game conventions, music festivals, whatever!

Instead of promoting them as places where people can come to meet their prospective partners (you’ll be accused of trying to resurrect the Single, Desperate, and Ugly club), let’s bet that happy and fulfilled people with friends and access to thriving third spaces will couple up if they want to.

Instead of ramming pro-fertility rhetoric down our throats, let’s focus instead on eroding the barriers that so many people feel when it comes to being part of a community, like the steep cost of just existing in public in capitalist Singapore or the exorbitant cost of late night transportation or the reality that it’s hard to have friends over (let alone a prospective date) when one is expected to live with their family until their 30s.

Let’s focus on broadening the extremely narrow horizon of social possibility in Singapore, where everyone complains that there is no nature, no culture, and nothing to do but eat and sleep and travel. Is it any wonder that an earlier prototype of FirstDate places such a big emphasis on free first meals? What else is there to do?

If this sounds like a radical solution to you, it’s only because you haven’t been paying attention, because it’s already happening.

It offers a fascinating window into what government-funded culture activities that are also not-so-secretly trying to get people to make babies could look like. Festival attendees were literally handed out bracelets to signal to other attendees their openness to a relationship, and yet, the reception from everyone I spoke to was almost unanimously positive (towards the event, not the bracelets).

In a time of shuttering nightclubs, bookstores, theatre groups, and whatever else you’d consider a common social space, I’d argue that this kind of support is badly needed. And, I would wager that MSF’s bet on third spaces is more likely to produce happy couples (and babies, if you care about that) than this.

Let the cosplayers meet their kindred souls at the government-funded con. Let the book lovers meet at the talk at the indie bookstore. And let the nightlife enthusiasts meet at the sober (or not so sober) rave.

And if you don’t get the love of your life out of it, well, at least you’ll have had a good time doing it.

items.title: The death of web development education
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
In a personal blog post, Baldur Bjarnason describes how he worked in various fields and positions: as an author, publisher, consultant, developer, educator, as well as radio and TV producer. None of these jobs were economically viable in the long term.

Adding insult to injury, the respective communities alienate interdisciplinary people who do not fit into their narrow conception of the field. For example, either you are considered as too “technical” for a “creative” job or too “creative” for “technical” job.

Bjarnason describes the impact of generative AI on web development education:

[All] my training and education projects had dropped off one by one. Most of my peers who had been selling courses and training were shutting down their businesses. The demand for web dev ebooks had cratered. […]

Software developers haven’t all switched to using agents for their coding, but they do seem to have all switched to error-prone, backwards-facing, nondeterministic chatbots for what now passes as web dev “education”.

Many independent educators who used to earn a living from web development training and developer relations have reported that GenAI has ruined their business.

The income from my book sales went from being enough for me to live off (2024) to zero (2026).

The traffic to my blog and my books (which were free to read online) increased beyond what I can currently afford. Virtually all of it comes from AI crawlers, so there is no ad income.

Therefore, I’m taking my blog and my books offline so that I can decide what to do next – especially w.r.t. AI companies stealing my work.

[Developers] aren’t gathering together in online spaces to learn and teach and share exciting projects anymore, rather they are mindlessly scrolling for a much-needed hit of short-form content dopamine (because the horrors of the world are more persistent than ever). […] [Many] developers have replaced authentic human collaboration with conversations with the dreaded Chat Bots. […]

The future feels bleak for educators. Rich curriculums we craft intentionally and carefully for real human audiences are now routinely stolen and regurgitated by predictive algorithms. The Chat Bots, with their sycophantic tone of voice, are deliberately engineered to erase our own personalities, hard work and craft entirely from the equation.

The only conclusion I can draw from this is that my experience, skills, empathy and teaching expertise no longer hold the value they once did in this volatile industry (if they ever really did?).

Alam-Naylor decided to accept a lower-paid developer job without public exposure. She decided to go offline.

I’ve spoken to a few course creators now, and we’re all seeing the same trend. Revenue down 50%+. Fewer people engaging with our content. People switching to LLMs, which slurp up all of our work and regurgitate it, without consent or compensation.

Comeau notes that with LLMs, there’s no incentive for people to make high-quality free content.

I’m making half the money I was making exactly one year ago. [This] is definitely not sustainable for a full-time job. […] [There’s] almost no incentive as a creator of content to create programming content when it makes practically no money and is incredibly difficult to make when I could just make a video about the latest AI model, which is easy to make, makes more money, and gets more views. […] There’s almost no reason to make programming content anymore. The only reason I do it is because I find value in it. I find enjoyment in it. And I’m able to make money through other means rather than just YouTube ad revenue.

Rachel Andrew is a renowned technical writer and editor of many books and articles on web topics. In a series of blog posts, she reflects on the impact of GenAI on technical publishing. She reports that GenAI has broken the relationship between subject matter experts – the authors of the original draft – and editors who proof-read, fact-check and polish the article.

Editors have to apply extra scrutiny because AI tools might have introduced subtle inaccuracies without the original authors being aware of it. AI can be very confidently wrong, and if the text seems clear, it’s possible to miss that it’s clearly nonsense. Authors want to save some time, but create additional work for the editing team.

She further questions whether AI actually increases productivity. Potential productivity gains stem from GenAI automating certain tasks. These tasks can as well be automated without AI, Andrew says, AI just makes it more accessible to non-coders. Now that more information, like API references, is made available in a machine-readable format for LLMs, it’s easier to perform non-AI automations.

Again Andrew argues that perceived individual productivity benefits might come from shifting the work onto someone else. For example, writers shift the work onto technical editors or even the readers. [You] might feel more productive, but all you’ve done is move the work around, make someone else’s job or experience measurably worse, and reduce quality. In summary, she asks (emphasis mine):

How can we justify the cost (financial, environmental, and human) of AI, if the reality is a relatively small bump in productivity that could have happened by to automate tasks using existing tools or simple coding? Why aren’t businesses encouraging people to use non-AI methods where possible, saving the AI only for where it adds value? Given the societal costs, and the benefit to a business of bringing onboard and training people, perhaps on a balance of things even those tasks where AI is needed are better performed by people.

First and foremost, I would like to acknowledge these experiences and amplify these voices. GenAI has catastrophic effects on web development education and learning. It threatens the livelihoods of writers, teachers and communicators who make web technologies approachable and accessible, who nurture the next generation of web authors and developers.

There is no obvious short-term solution. This does not stop some people from posting knee-jerk reactions. I won’t link to these blog posts, but they go like this:

  • They advice to ”adapt” to GenAI and “agentic” development and to “come to terms” with the new situation.
  • They want to cheer people up by saying “you’ll get used to it”, “you’ll find a new role” – even if the role is cleaning up slop.
  • They argue: “You cannot expect the field not to change”. “AI is here to stay.”

These reactions are in essence the same as “you gotta jump on the AI train or you’ll perish”. Such comments are merely turning the knife in the wound.

I cannot give those educators any advice. But I do imagine a more compassionate reaction:

I highly appreciate your work as an educator, writer, researcher, or free and open-source software developer. A heartfelt thank you. I am sorry that AI sucks all joy out of you and your profession.

I acknowledge that AI companies appropriate your labor, destroy your economic livelihood and threaten the foundations of your field.

This very situation won’t get better with more AI, better AI, or developing with or for AI.

In a situation where Big Tech teamed up with fascist movements, it sounds far-fetched, but the bare minimum would be to force the AI oligarchs to pay for the crisis they are imposing on the web community, among others. We need to expropriate the expropriators.

Against the destruction of web development education, I’d like to hold up certain values. In a previous blog post, I described how I once entered web development through a volunteer-driven, non-commercial documentation project.

Such initiatives the web as they helped a wide range of people to establish their own web sites and communities – local businesses, self-employed professionals, art and craft groups, neighborhood initiatives, schools and kindergartens, sports clubs, LGBTQ+ folks, fandoms etc.

Today, we often hear the word “democratize” from GenAI promoters, but it means the exact opposite. AI centralizes power and commodifies knowledge, instead of teaching skills and deep understanding.

The web is a radical democratic medium. Right now, tech oligarchs and fascist movements are trying to dismantle its radical potential. We must ensure that everyone can shape the web.

Participating in independent learning communities, using open technologies based on ethical principles, and building a shared and inclusive digital infrastructure is an act of self-empowerment and emancipation.

Humans need to have the resources to learn, research and teach web publishing skills. It is humans who do all the essential knowledge and education work, and they need to be paid for it.

This sounds trite, but GenAI advocates do not acknowledge it. They let Big Tech get away with appropriating the work of web educators. We cannot make concessions here.

I don’t enjoy my field any more because the field is gone. Assuming that there’s still something there is a mistake. That feeling you have isn’t a frustration with changes to your chosen field. It’s nostalgia for a field that disappeared overnight. What passes as web dev today at large bears no resemblance to the field we built over the years. Everything we learned has been abandoned because companies assume it’s all been encoded into their chosen Large Language Model.

Assuming that’s true, I am guilty of nostalgia. I just believe in a resilient web that is not that easy to lock in a cage. To rebuild the field of web development, it requires a network of people who support each other, get a grip on web technologies, dig out best practices and establish new ones, and share their insights.

Version 3.0 of SvelteKit, the official application framework for Svelte, is now available.

If you’ve used earlier versions of SvelteKit, everything will feel very familiar — it’s the same framework with a little more polish, a little more type safety, and a little less junk. We’ve made migration as seamless as we can with the command...

...which will automatically migrate as much of your codebase as possible, and generate a TODO list for everything else. (If you’re agentically inclined, your robot friends will make short work of it.)

  • configuration now lives in instead of
  • error handling is improved across the board

Not quite. But it’s our top priority!

Remote functions are a set of utilities for secure, efficient, type-safe client-server communication. You’ve likely seen some version of this idea in other frameworks, but we think you’re going to prefer this one.

Using them requires Async Svelte, which for now requires an flag. Bear with us.

This is as good a place as any to remind everyone that the next in-person Svelte Summit is taking place on November 19-20 in the lovely town of Ljubljana, Slovenia. Among other things it will be a celebration of Svelte’s 10th birthday, and we’d love to share some cake with you.

items.content:
Today we are proudly shipping Pi 1.0: a hardened, minimal, extensible agent harness that you can make your own. Hundreds of thousands of people around the world use Pi every week. Many of you submit issues and pull requests. Over the course of many months, we have used that feedback to improve, harden and evolve Pi into a stable piece of software that people and businesses can depend on.

Pi is known for being minimal. We care about holding that line. While agentic tooling changes every week, many of the changes do not last. Pi does not work that way. We wait until something has proven itself, and only then do we consider adopting it; weighing its true functionality against its inherent added complexity. We spoke more about that process and how it relates to Codemode and MCP earlier this week here.

The Pi 1.0 we are shipping today is a result of that process. Pi already ran the latest models from every major provider, became a daily driver coding agent for people around the world, and provided a supermalleable substrate on which to build agentic applications. With Pi 1.0 we are adding the following into Pi:

  • Codemode (native support for MCP, and non-LLM models like Jev and image models)
  • Extension support for virtual models
  • Cache warming for anthropic models
  • Mid-conversation system messages (transcript-aware prompt and tool changes)
  • Full-screen mode by default

We have thought about many of these features for months. They were thrown up against the wall and stuck. The list of things that fell off the wall is much longer. When we use Pi with all these new features it feels like a major step forward, but it also still feels simple, like Pi.

Alongside this work of continually refining and evolving Pi, we also began to understand that there were aspects of Pi that did not fit the shape of how many people wanted to use it. At Earendil, we want to bring Pi's minimalism and the way it allows you to wield AI outside of the coding agent and outside of the terminal. It needs to be reachable from different surfaces and support longer-running conversations and tasks. In short, Pi must become more durable. Rather than stray from our minimal roots and try to make Pi something it wasn't, we combined that work into a new experimental package that we are shipping today, Pi Durable. Pi Durable is a new substrate for building long-running agentic applications that lets the builders and the users of those applications wield and steer the underlying intelligence with tremendous dexterity. It shares Pi's key principles, minimalism and supermalleability, but it extends those principles into new dimensions. Mario writes in more detail about how we crafted Pi Durable here.

Earendil was formed to craft software and open protocols that strengthen human agency. Today we are shipping tools to you all to help do just that. We're eager to hear feedback from you and to harness the future out in the open together.

Pi 1.0 is available today:

curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh

powershell -c

Pi Durable is available today as an experimental package:

npm install @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/chord

items.content:
Today Earendil and the Pi community shipped Pi 1.0. This reflects our belief that after countless hours of hardening, maintenance, and active development, Pi is now a solid foundation on which to build. Pi also continues to evolve. Together with Pi 1.0, we are shipping an experimental new package called Pi Durable. Pi Durable was built specifically for long-running, durable, and malleable agents that can run anywhere. We would like you to join in the fun and help us make it the best durable harness there is.

Pi the coding agent is built to run on your (remote) machine, inside a terminal, driven by one person. If the process dies, you look at what happened and tell it to continue. That is what Pi 1.0 focuses on and excels at, and that is not changing.

At Earendil, we want to bring this technology to everyone, in whatever form fits their needs best. For that, we need a harness that runs anywhere, can be reached from different surfaces, supports infinitely long conversations, survives catastrophic internal and external failures, and lets multiple humans steer the same agents.

Pi Durable is that harness. It does not replace the Pi coding agent. It is a framework for building any agentic application, coding agents included. It shares not only code with the Pi coding agent, like pi-ai, but also its principles: minimalism and malleability.

It also lets us explore designs in this space without disrupting Pi the coding agent. Lessons we learn building agentic applications on Pi Durable will flow back into Pi the coding agent as they prove themselves valuable.

Everybody has their own definition of a harness. We wrote about this previously, but let us reintroduce the concept of the harness for Pi Durable.

A harness is storage plus the machinery needed to run one or more conversations with large language models in parallel. It provides the tools those models call, and the execution environments the tools run in.

A conversation is an interaction between you and an agent, recorded as a transcript. The agent is the large language model together with its settings, like the thinking level, and the tools it can call.

Tools do their work through an execution environment, which can be your laptop, a remote VM, or an in-memory sandbox. Which tools and which execution environment an agent gets is up to each conversation.

Everything the harness runs, from calling the model to executing a tool, is a task.

Like everything in Pi, Pi Durable is built so your agent can understand it. The entire source code, without tests, is about 15,000 lines, which comes out to about 150,000 tokens with GPT and about 250,000 with Claude. That's the worst case. To build on Pi Durable, your agent rarely needs all of it; the storage backends alone are 3,000 lines it can usually skip.

Now let us give you a little tour of Pi Durable, to illustrate what we built and why we built it.

We want agents to run for a long time and to be able to run anywhere, where anywhere currently means anywhere there is a JavaScript runtime.

In Pi Durable, a harness opens over a storage backend. Pi Durable ships memory, SQLite, and JSONL storage, plus a conformance suite and benchmarks for your own backend. The SQLite and JSONL storage code uses no Node APIs, so with a small adapter it runs on Bun or inside a Cloudflare Durable Object. The storage interface is small and easy to implement on top of whatever you have, like a key-value store or Postgres. One process owns a storage at a time, and other clients attach to that process.

On SQLite, the harness only keeps the working set in memory: the active transcripts, live tasks, and pending submissions. Everything else stays on disk until it is needed. Active transcripts are naturally bounded by the model's context window, because compaction summarizes older messages before they overflow it. So even a conversation with tens of thousands of messages fits snugly into memory.

Tools that need files or a shell get them from an execution environment. Pi Durable ships a Node execution environment, which gives tools access to your local files. Like storage, the execution environment interface is small and easy to implement, so you can also expose remote execution environments to your tools. That allows the harness to run on one machine while its tools run on another. Your function builds the environment for every tool call, from the conversation's working directory, so each conversation can run in a different place.

 { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } ;
 { createModels } ;
 { openaiProvider } ;
 { createRegistry, Harness } ;
 { NodeExecutionEnv } ;
 {
    openNodeSqliteStorage,
} ;
 { CodingTools } ;

 context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT;  models = createModels();
models.setProvider(openaiProvider());

 registry = createRegistry();
registry.install(CodingTools);  env = ({ cwd }: { cwd?: string }) =>
     NodeExecutionEnv({ cwd: cwd ?? process.cwd() });
 harness =  Harness.open(
     openNodeSqliteStorage(),
    { models, registry, env },
    context,
);
 root =  harness.root(context, {
    agent: {
        model: { provider: , modelId:  },
        cwd: ,
    },
});

We want an agent to survive its process dying, whether the laptop sleeps, the container is redeployed, or the machine runs out of memory, and to pick up where it left off.

In Pi Durable, every step of a run is a task that stores a checkpoint before it moves on. If the process dies, a new process opens the same storage, finds the unfinished tasks, and continues each one from its last checkpoint. A model request that was cut off is sent again; the partial answer stays in the transcript, marked as aborted. A tool call that was cut off reruns if it is safe to; otherwise the model is told it was interrupted. Pi Durable has no built-in subagents, but they take a few lines of code to build, as the triage tool below shows. A subagent runs in a conversation of its own, so it continues from where it left off too, and a subagent tool that is safe to rerun finds its subagent again and waits for its answer. Queued messages are still queued. A makes a submission exactly-once, so a client that retries after a crash gets the original submission back instead of asking twice.

 job = {
    : ,
    content: ,
    requestId: ,
} ;
 root.submit(job, context);
 harness =  Harness.open(
     openNodeSqliteStorage(),
    { models, registry, env },
    context,
);
harness.resume();  root =  harness.root(context);
 settled =  ( root.submit(job, context)).wait(context);

Many conversations at once

We want one harness to run many conversations at the same time, without one blocking another.

In Pi Durable, one harness runs as many conversations as you need, concurrently, all with the same guarantees. A conversation starts fresh or forks another one at any point in its transcript, and sees the parent's history up to that point without copying it.

Think of a Slack channel where your agent answers mentions from anyone. Then somebody opens a thread. The channel can be one conversation, and the thread a fork of it at the message the thread replies to. Both run at the same time and neither blocks the other.

 channel =  harness.root(context);
 question =  channel.submit(
    { : , content:  },
    context,
);
 answered =  question.wait(context);

 thread =  channel.fork(
    answered.answer!,
    { ownership: { kind:  } },
    context,
);

 inThread =  thread.submit(
    { : , content:  },
    context,
);
 inChannel =  channel.submit(
    { : , content:  },
    context,
);
 Promise.all([inThread.wait(context), inChannel.wait(context)]);

Each conversation also stores its own agent: the model, the thinking level, the selected extensions and which of their tools are active, extra instructions, and the working directory in its execution environment. A reviewer next to the main agent can use a cheaper model, read-only tools, and its own checkout.

We want everything an agent can do to be pluggable, and every plugged-in piece to take part in durability.

In Pi Durable, an extension is a named bundle of system prompt sections, tools, hooks, and tasks. The application installs extensions in a registry. Each conversation selects which extensions and tools it uses, and stores only their names.

The system prompt is rebuilt from the sections of the conversation's extensions before every request, so a changed section is picked up by the next request. Pi Durable records what changed in the transcript, at the position where it changed, so a restart or a fork sees exactly what the model saw. On models that support system prompt and tool changes in the middle of a conversation, only the change is sent, so the prompt cache stays valid.

 { defineExtension, section } ;

 ProjectContext = defineExtension({
    name: ,
    sections: [
        
        section(, (input) => agentsMd.latest(input.env)),
        section(, (input) => skills.latest(input.env)),
    ],
});

Every tool call runs as its own durable task, and its intent is stored before it runs. After a crash, a tool reruns only if it says that is safe. Otherwise the model is told the call was interrupted, with the output stored so far, and decides what to do. Each conversation can also get its own set of tools, like the Slack thread from earlier, which may search but not deploy.

 { Type } ;
 { defineTool } ;

 searchIssues = defineTool({
    name: ,
    description: ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ query: Type.String() }),
    replay: , 
    execute: async (args, api) => {
        
        api.output(args.query);
         {
            content: [{ : , text: await tracker.search(args.query) }],
        };
    },
});

 deploy = defineTool({
    name: ,
    description: ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ version: Type.String() }),
    
    execute: async (args) => ({
        content: [{ : , text: await ci.deploy(args.version) }],
    }),
});

registry.install(defineExtension({ name: , tools: [searchIssues, deploy] }));

 thread.configure({ tools: { remove: [deploy] } }, context);

A tool gets the harness API for its call: it can commit entries and documents, start tasks and conversations, and talk to other conversations. That makes a subagent a few lines of code. A tool creates a conversation it owns, gives it a smaller model and its own instructions, and waits for its answer. The subagent is a conversation like any other, so it survives a crash, counts its own cost, and a UI can show it under the call.

 { AssistantMessage } ;
 { AssistantEntry, configure } ;

 triage = defineTool({
    name: ,
    description: ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ issue: Type.String() }),
    
    replay: ,
    execute: async (args, api, context) => {
         child =  api.commit( (tx) => {
             existing = (
                 tx.scanConversations({ ownerTaskId: api.taskId }, )
            ).items[];
             (existing !== )  existing.id;
             created =  tx.createConversation({
                ownership: { kind: , taskId: api.taskId },
            });
             configure(tx, created.id, {
                model: { provider: , modelId:  },
                tools: [],
                instructions: ,
            });
             created.id;
        }, context);
         api.details({ conversationId: child }, context);
         subagent =  api.conversation(child, context);
         request = {
            : ,
            content: args.issue,
            requestId: api.taskId,
        } ;
         settled =  (
             subagent!.submit(request, context)
        ).wait(context);
         entry =  api.commit(
            (tx) => tx.entry(AssistantEntry, settled.answer!),
            context,
        );
         message = entry?.model?.[]  AssistantMessage;
         text = message.content
            .flatMap((content) => (content. ===  ? [content.text] : []))
            .join();
         { content: [{ : , text }] };
    },
});

Extensions can also change other extensions' tools. A tool with the same name in a later extension replaces the earlier one, for example a bash that runs inside a Python virtualenv. A wrap decorates whichever tool won, wherever the wrapping extension is selected.

 { wrapTool } ;
 { createBashTool } ;

 Timing = defineExtension({
    name: ,
    wraps: [
        wrapTool(createBashTool(), (bash) => ({
            ...bash,
            execute: async (args, api, context) => {
                 start = Date.now();
                 {
                     bash.execute(args, api, context);
                }  {
                    metrics.record(, Date.now() - start);
                }
            },
        })),
    ],
});

Hooks let extensions step into tasks, including the built-in tasks for generating a model response, invoking a tool, or performing compaction. They can rewrite a request before it goes to the model, block or rewrite a tool call, replace a result, keep a run going, or write a summary themselves. A hook can run again after a crash, so a hook that makes a decision stores it in a memo: a small value stored with the task, where the first write wins.

 { hook, ToolTask } ;

 Approval = defineExtension({
    name: ,
    hooks: [
        hook(ToolTask, {
            beforeTool: async (call, api, context) => {
                 (call.name !== ) ;
                 approved =  api.memo<boolean>(
                    ,
                    context,
                );
                approved ??=  api.memo(
                    ,
                     askInSlack(call),
                    context,
                );
                 approved
                    ? 
                    : { block:  };
            },
        }),
    ],
});

Several extensions can hook the same thing. Their hooks run as a chain, in the order the conversation selects the extensions, and each hook defines how its chain runs. passes rewritten arguments down the chain, and the first block stops it. passes the result down the chain. stops at the first hook that keeps the run going. Observers like always run them all. A hook that throws is reported, and the chain continues, except in , where a throw blocks the call.

The harness runs conversations with built-in tasks: one for each model request, one for each tool call, and one for compaction. Extensions bring their own tasks and get the same machinery: a checkpoint after every step, timers that survive restarts, and waiting on other tasks.

A checkout that splits the bill across several cards charges every card at once. If one card is declined, the other payments are aborted and refund themselves:

 Payment = defineTask<{ card: string }, { phase:  }, string>({
    name: ,
    version: 1,
    initial: () => ({ phase:  }),
    phases: {
        charge: async (task, runtime, context) => {
             charge =  bank.charge(
                task.input.card,
                task.id,
            );
             runtime.commit(
                () => ({

            );
        },
    },
    
    abort: async (task, runtime, context) => {
         bank.refund(task.id);
         runtime.commit(
            () => ({ status: , outcome: { status:  } }),
            context,
        );
    },
});

    | { phase: ; payments: TaskId<string>[] };

    name: ,
    version: 1,
    initial: () => ({ phase:  }),
    phases: {
        pay: async (task, runtime, context) => {
             runtime.commit( (tx) => {
                 payments: TaskId<string>[] = [];

                    status: ,

            );

                (outcome) => outcome.status === ,

                        ? { status: , result:  }

                            status: ,

    name: ,
    description: ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ cards: Type.Array(Type.String()) }),
    execute: async (args, api, context) => {
         owner = {
            ownership: { kind: , taskId: api.taskId },
        } ;
         id =  api.createTask(
            Checkout,
            { cards: args.cards },
            owner,
            context,
        );
         { outcome } = ( api.waitForTask(id, context)).state;
         text =
            outcome.status ===  ? outcome.result : outcome.status;
         { content: [{ : , text }] };

registry.install(defineExtension({
    name: ,
    tools: [checkout],
    tasks: [Payment, Checkout],

Tasks and conversations form one ownership tree. Aborting a task aborts what it owns, bottom-up, so every task cleans up its own effects first, and a task only finishes once the work it owns has finished. A subagent is the same pattern: a conversation owned by the tool call that started it.

Tasks are foreground by default: they are part of the conversation's current work. The conversation is idle only once they are done, and aborting the conversation, for example when the user presses Esc, aborts them and everything they own. A background task belongs to the conversation, but not to its current work. The conversation goes idle while it runs, and an ordinary abort leaves it and everything it owns alone. That fits a subagent that should outlive the turn that started it, or a reminder that fires tomorrow. Aborting the task itself, or the conversation with , still stops it.

 api.createTask(
    Checkout,
    input,
    { ownership: { kind: , taskId: api.taskId } },
    context,
);

 api.createTask(
    Reminder,
    input,
    { ownership: { kind:  }, background: true },
    context,
);

We want long conversations to keep going without the agent stopping to summarize.

In Pi Durable, compaction is a task like any other, and it runs while the conversation keeps going. When the context gets close to the model's limit, a background compaction summarizes the older messages, and the summary is placed at the next turn boundary. The conversation only waits for a summary when the next request would not fit otherwise. If the provider still rejects a request as too long, the harness compacts and retries once. You can also compact manually at any time, with your own instructions. The older messages always stay in storage.

 harness =  Harness.open(storage, {
    models,
    registry,
    settings: {
        compaction: {
            
            reserveTokens: 16384,
            
            backgroundTokens: 32768,
        },
    },
}, context);

 root.compact(, context);

goes further: it starts a new context, optionally from a handoff note, and a tool can ask for the same by returning . Because nothing is deleted, a second tool can still search everything before the handoff. That is all it takes to build an agent that hands off to itself and looks things up later.

 handoff = defineTool({
    name: ,
    description:
         +
        ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ note: Type.String() }),
    execute: async (args, api, context) => {
         self =  api.conversation(api.conversationId, context);
         self!.submit(
            {
                : ,
                content: ,
                requestId: api.taskId,
            },
            context,
        );
         {
            content: [{ : , text:  }],
            control: { handoff: args.note },
        };
    },
});

 searchHistory = defineTool({
    name: ,
    description: ,
    parameters: Type.Object({ text: Type.String() }),
    replay: ,
    execute: async (args, api, context) => {
         page =  api.commit(
            (tx) => tx.scanEntries({ conversationId: api.conversationId }, ),
            context,
        );
         hits = page.items.filter((entry) =>
            JSON.stringify(entry.model ?? []).includes(args.text),
        );
         text = hits.map((entry) => JSON.stringify(entry.model)).join();
         { content: [{ : , text }] };
    },
});

Durable application state

We want the state of the application built on the agent to be as durable as the conversation itself.

In Pi Durable, application state, like a todo list, a plan, a ticket, or the sandbox a conversation runs in, lives in documents. Documents are typed JSON stored next to the transcript and changed in the same atomic commits, so the state never disagrees with the transcript that produced it. Each document says what a fork starts with: the parent's value at the fork point, its current value, or a fresh one.

 { defineDoc } ;

 Todos = defineDoc<{ items: string[] }>({
    kind: ,
    version: 1,
    scope: ,
    history: ,
    fork: , 
    initial: () => ({ items: [] }),
});

 Todo = defineExtension({
    name: ,
    tools: [
        defineTool({
            name: ,
            description: ,
            parameters: Type.Object({ item: Type.String() }),
            execute: async (args, api, context) => {
                 api.commit( (tx) => {
                     todos =  tx.doc(Todos, api.conversationId);
                    todos.items.push(args.item);
                }, context);
                 text = args.item;
                 { content: [{ : , text }] };
            },
        }),
    ],
    
    sections: [
        section(,  (input, context) => {
             todos =  input.read.snapshot(
                Todos,
                input.conversationId,
                context,
            );
             todos?.items.join() || ;
        }),
    ],
});

 todos =  harness.documentState(Todos, channel.id, context);
todos?.subscribe((value) => renderTodos(value?.items ?? []));

We want to change the code of a running agent without stopping it.

In Pi Durable, the registry can change while conversations run. Installing an extension under a name that is already installed replaces it in one step. A tool call that is already running finishes on the code it started with; the next call uses the new code. Conversations store extension and tool names, never code, so after a restart they pick up whatever the new process installs.


registry.install( loadExtension());

We want many people and clients to work with the same conversations at once: watch them, join late, and steer them.

In Pi Durable, everything a UI needs is committed state, so any number of clients can attach to any conversation in the harness. A client gets the current view first: the transcript, the answer being streamed, running tools and their output, queued messages, the agent, and usage. After that it only gets what changes. A client that joins late or reconnects starts from the current view. Any client can steer a running conversation or queue a follow-up.

 view =  thread.viewState(context);
render(view.value);
view.subscribe((value) => render(value));

 thread.submit(
    { : , content: , whenBusy:  },
    context,
);

For a remote client, delivers the exact operations of every commit, small enough to send over a socket. If you prefer the coding agent's familiar events, turns the commits into those, at the cost of more bytes on the wire.

The vacation planner is about 1,300 lines of TypeScript, most of them the TUI. If it looks like a coding agent, that's only because it borrows its TUI components from the Pi coding agent.

To run both demos from a Pi checkout:

npm install && npm run build
node packages/coding-agent/src/experimental/durable/main.ts
node packages/coding-agent/src/experimental/vacation/main.ts

To build on Pi Durable in your own project:

npm install @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/chord

In the coming weeks, we will talk more about Pi Durable and show you the small agentic tools we build with it to help us work, like a Slack bot or a GitHub triage bot. We don't want to spill the beans yet. There is more coming as we use Pi Durable ourselves, just like we use Pi.

Because it is the easiest way to bootstrap this. But as everybody knows by now, it's very easy to port everything to Rust or assembler. We're not ruling this out in the future, but at the moment we are focusing on TypeScript.
